evidence: The Design maps all seven acceptance outcomes to owned boundaries, public entry points, exact selectors, non-happy refusals, rollback, and compatibility paths without evident scope creep. Product changes are required because the acceptance criteria are compound and the delivery outcome lacks a complete success-metric decision contract.

findings.issue: AC1-AC7 each combine multiple independently passable capabilities and refusal cases into one acceptance criterion; for example AC1 combines inventory completeness, authority prohibition, static proof, behavioral proof, and two gate outcomes.
findings.why: A compound criterion can be partially satisfied and still reported as met, so the seven-outcome map does not provide singular pass/fail acceptance boundaries.
findings.suggestion: Keep the seven product outcomes and wave ceiling, but give each AC a closed checklist of singular normative assertions with an explicit all-assertions-must-pass aggregation rule; bind each existing exact selector to one assertion rather than treating the whole paragraph as one testable thought.

findings.issue: The quality targets are implementation conformance thresholds, but the Design does not define the baseline, observation window, guardrail, and keep/iterate/remove decision rule for the user outcome that this corrective wave is intended to improve.
findings.why: Passing selectors can show the controls exist, but cannot settle whether governed delivery actually reduces the four P0 failure modes without unacceptable impact on successful completion or operator effort.
findings.suggestion: Add a bounded post-wave outcome contract: baseline P0 incidence and successful-wave completion/operator-cost measure, target threshold, measurement window, guardrail, and an explicit decision rule for retaining, iterating, or reverting the corrective controls.
